chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from Jamil ibn Darraj from Mansur ibn Hazim who said:

Indeed, the Mu'la is compelled to issue a final divorce. The rationale in these two reports, although the source in both is one (namely, Mansur ibn Hazim), is to interpret them as referring to the one whom the Imam sees fit to compel to issue a final divorce due to a certain consideration of interest, without that being obligatory in every Mu'la who is divorced.

key_terms.الْمُؤْلَى: A man who divorces his wife three times in one sitting
key_terms.بِشَاهِدِ الْحَالِ: Based on the state of affairs / circumstances
key_terms.طَلِيقَةً بَائِنَةً: A final divorce that makes the wife unlawful to remarry without a new contract
key_terms.لِضَرْبٍ مِنَ الْمَصْلَحَةِ: For a certain consideration of interest

ai.seo_question: Is the Mu'la always obligated to issue a final divorce, or is it at the Imam's discretion?
ai.summary: In al-Istibsar, Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Mansur ibn Hazim to clarify the juristic principle that compelling a Mu'la to issue a final divorce is a discretionary administrative act (takhayyuri) by the Imam based on public interest (maslahah), rather than an intrinsic legal obligation (wajib) inherent to the status itself. This distinction highlights the Shia emphasis on the Imam's authority to adapt rulings to specific circumstances, ensuring the divorce serves its intended purpose of severing ties definitively when necessary.
